items.title: Who Is the Mexican Drug Kingpin Known as El Chapo Isidro?
items.summary: The kingpin, Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, was captured in a violent operation in Mexico. He was one of the F.B.I.’s 10 most wanted fugitives.
items.full_text:
Title: Who Is the Mexican Drug Kingpin Known as El Chapo Isidro? - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/21/world/americas/mexico-el-chapo-isidro-drug-kingpin.html

Published Time: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 16:30:49 GMT

Markdown Content:
Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, a Mexican drug kingpin who was one of the United States’ most wanted criminals, [has been captured](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/21/world/americas/mexico-el-chapo-isidro-captured-drugs.html), the Mexican government said on Saturday.

Mr. Meza Flores, known as El Chapo Isidro, was among the most powerful drug traffickers in Sinaloa, a state in northwestern Mexico where cartels mass produce fentanyl and other illicit drugs that are bound for the United States and other parts of the world.

The U.S. authorities have described Mr. Meza Flores as a top drug trafficker in the region who leads the Meza-Flores organization, a heavily armed and violent group. He was first indicted in the United States over a decade ago, and he has been on the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s [10 Most Wanted Fugitives](https://www.fbi.gov/wanted/topten) list since last year.

Here’s what we know about the drug kingpin.

## How did he become so powerful?

Mr. Meza Flores, 44, appears to have worked his way up through the ranks of Mexico’s drug cartels. He was a leader of the Beltrán Leyva drug trafficking organization, which split from the Sinaloa Cartel in 2008, according to the Treasury Department.

The Sinaloa Cartel, which was founded and led by Joaquin Guzmán Loera, known as El Chapo, and Ismael Zambada Garcia, known as El Mayo, is one of the world’s largest and most feared crime syndicates. Rivalries among cartels and organizations that splintered off during internal fighting have led to [devastating gang](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/06/30/world/americas/sinaloa-cartel-mexico.html) wars in Mexico.

(Mr. Meza Flores shares a similar nickname but is not related to Mr. Guzmán Loera, who was arrested in 2014.)

Image

A handout photograph showing Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, also known as El Chapo Isidro.Credit...F.B.I., via Getty Images-Agence France-Presse

The Beltrán Leyva split set off a bloody regional war[, according to the Treasury Department](https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/jy1952), which issued sanctions against the group. Beltrán Leyva was [founded](https://www.state.gov/narcotics-rewards-program-target-information-brought-to-justice/marcos-arturo-beltran-leyva-deceased) by Arturo Beltran Leyva, a weapons and drug smuggler, and [his brothers](https://www.wilsoncenter.org/beltran-leyva-organization-blo), and its enforcement arm is considered “one of the most ruthless and brutal in the way they dispose of their enemies,” according to [the State Department](https://www.state.gov/narcotics-rewards-program-target-information-brought-to-justice/marcos-arturo-beltran-leyva-deceased).

Mr. Meza Flores later became the leader of his own group, the Meza-Flores criminal organization.

## What is his group accused of?

The Meza-Flores group has smuggled tons of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine and marijuana into the United States from several places in Mexico, according to U.S. officials. The group has long operated from the northern city of Guasave in Sinaloa, U.S. officials say.

In 2013, the Treasury Department officially designated Mr. Meza Flores and his group as a drug trafficking organization and [linked](https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/tg1824) Mr. Meza Flores’s wife, parents, sister and uncles to the criminal enterprise.

Mr. Meza Flores waged a brutal turf war with the Sinaloa Cartel, which saw the quadrupling of drug-related killings between roughly 2008 and 2012, as well as a spike in kidnappings and arson attacks, the Treasury Department said in 2013.

But the Meza-Flores group had recently allied with a faction of the cartel that has been fighting for control, according to Adrián López, the publisher of a leading newspaper in Sinaloa’s state capital that has closely covered the cartel wars.

The Meza-Flores group is responsible for the deaths of many Mexican police officers as well as military and law enforcement officials, according to the F.B.I.

## How long has the U.S. sought him?

Mr. Meza Flores was indicted in May 2012 in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia on charges related to the possession and distribution of cocaine and methamphetamine. In 2019, a federal grand jury issued a new indictment for him with additional drug trafficking charges, and firearms violations.

Last year the F.B.I. added Mr. Meza Flores to its 10 Most Wanted Fugitives List, offering a reward of up to $5 million for information leading to his capture.

Federal prosecutors in Washington updated the charges against Mr. Meza Flores two months ago, suggesting that the U.S. authorities were still actively pursuing him. The latest indictment added new counts, including terrorism charges accusing Mr. Meza Flores of acting in support of the Sinaloa Cartel, and it accused him of abducting and killing a member of the Mexican National Guard in Oaxaca in 2022.

## How was he captured?

Mexico’s defense ministry [said in a statement](https://www.gob.mx/defensa/prensa/fuerzas-especiales-de-la-guardia-nacional-y-del-ejercito-detienen-a-fausto-n-a-chapo-isidro) on Saturday that the operation had been carried out in coordination with U.S. agencies.

The Drug Enforcement Administration said in a statement that the capture of Mr. Meza Flores “delivers a significant blow to a ruthless criminal organization” and “underscores the critical importance of intelligence sharing in targeting dangerous cartel leaders.”

Representatives for the State Department and the F.B.I. did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The operation to capture Mr. Meza Flores threw Guasave into turmoil on Friday night. Sinaloa State’s public security agency [urged](https://x.com/sspsinaloa1/status/2123976582003826892) residents to shelter in place and stay away from a major highway connecting the northern and southern parts of the state to avoid attacks between gang members and federal forces.

Paulina Villegas and Alan Feuer contributed reporting.

items.title: Anthropic’s Debut Shows the Disconnect Between Wall Street and Silicon Valley
items.summary: The A.I. giant broke records with its initial public offering this week before a rocky first full day of trading, as the markets plunged on worries about artificial intelligence spending.
items.full_text:
Title: Anthropic’s Debut Shows the Disconnect Between Wall Street and Silicon Valley - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/21/business/anthropic-stock-wall-street-silicon-valley.html

Published Time: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 16:27:33 GMT

Markdown Content:
Anthropic on Thursday celebrated its [first day of trading](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/19/technology/anthropic-2-trillion.html) as stock prices surged and the company touched a valuation of $2 trillion. On Friday, its stock deflated, sinking 9 percent.

In the aftermath of its record-breaking initial public offering, Anthropic, which makes the Claude chatbot, has vacuumed up [more than $120 billion in investor funds](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/18/technology/anthropic-ipo-pricing.html). It also consumed the good will of investors, many of whom were already becoming spooked at the artificial intelligence industry’s trillions of dollars of spending on data centers and other infrastructure to power the technology.

Following the huge investments in Anthropic, rival OpenAI and other A.I start-ups may face new hurdles going public, analysts and investors said. And even more established A.I. companies which need to raise debt or equity to pay for their expansion projects may encounter an uphill battle as the sector loses its glow.

That new hesitation was on full display this week, reflecting the widening disconnect between Silicon Valley optimism over A.I.’s potential and Wall Street’s growing doubts about whether the businesses are financially viable.

“The old-school way of looking at this is: This is the largest I.P.O. in history, late in the A.I. cycle. Psychologically, that could be a topping event,” said Michael O’Rourke, chief market strategist at JonesTrading, which brokers stock sales for hedge funds.

The market was shaken on Friday by some of those fears, ending the week with the worst stock slide in more than a year. The tech-heavy Nasdaq composite fell 5.3 percent, wiping away the gains it had made this year. And the S&P 500 fell 3.7 percent, reaching correction territory, or a drop of 10 percent from its recent high.

Stocks of bellwether A.I. companies including Nvidia, CoreWeave and Advanced Micro Devices fell by double-digit percentages on Friday.

Contributing to the sell-off was last week’s resignation of Jensen Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia, and worries about what that means for the chip maker’s important role financing other A.I. companies. Interest rates are also rising, making it more expensive for some companies to build data centers and buy chips. And Democrats swept into power during the midterm elections, many promising A.I. regulation.

Those developments put the enormous amount of money needed to finance the chips, data centers and electricity underpinning the technology at risk. Companies are planning to spend about $5 trillion between now and 2030 on the infrastructure, said Michael Arougheti, chief executive of Ares Management, a large investment manager, on an earnings call last month.

SpaceX, Meta and others tapped the markets last month for tens of billions of dollars to fuel their A.I. spending. Executives at most tech giants have told investors they are increasing their spending on the technology each quarter. And Anthropic’s initial public offering piled on top, causing fatigue, analysts and investors said.

Many concerns about A.I. spending are easily dismissed in Silicon Valley, which, by nature, lives in a different world. Venture capitalists this year have minted nearly 200 new unicorns, or start-ups worth more than $1 billion, more than in any other year since the private market frenzy in 2021, according to PitchBook, which tracks start-ups.

But a market for the kinds of initial public offerings or mergers to justify the velocity of investments hasn't yet emerged.

Even in Anthropic’s case, the company allowed early employees to sell more than $25 billion of combined stock at the start of trading, an unusually large sum that some investors and analysts viewed as aggressive. Companies and their investment bankers usually limit employees and other shareholders from selling their stock for weeks or months after I.P.O.s to help stabilize the price.

Many hedge fund managers failed to get stock in Anthropic’s offering at the initial price of $83 per share, said Raphaëlle D’Ornano, an A.I. industry analyst who also invests in public stocks. The hedge funds instead paid a significantly higher price for shares when trading opened on Thursday at $111.50.

Those hedge funds would have lost money as the stock quickly sank, closing at $88.91 on Friday. At the same time, funds have been trying to limit how much stock they own in A.I. companies overall, she added.

Friday “was pure panic,” Ms. D’Ornano said.

Wall Street and Silicon Valley largely agree that A.I. tools are certain to upend how people work, use the internet, and maybe even make discoveries in medicine. But no one is confident on how quickly the technology will produce those benefits.

And as the tech companies invest heavily, it isn’t clear how many will bring in enough revenue to become profitable. Anthropic’s rapid revenue growth has depended on businesses that use Claude for automating software engineering work, and the company will need to broaden that customer base in the coming years, analysts said.

OpenAI, which has filed for an initial public offering expected as soon as next year, is hoping for a similar shift into a broader customer base. The company also wants to get more free users of its popular chatbot, ChatGPT, to start paying.

(The New York Times has [sued OpenAI and Microsoft](https://www.nytimes.com/2023/12/27/business/media/new-york-times-open-ai-microsoft-lawsuit.html), claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)

Those business realities have led to some criticism from Wall Street fund managers, who feel that many in Silicon Valley are overly optimistic about potential returns. For example, Dylan Patel, a closely followed A.I. industry analyst, has predicted unrelenting growth, saying Anthropic and OpenAI would together surpass a half-trillion dollars in revenue by the end of next year, despite shaky markets.

As Mr. Patel walked onstage at a private San Francisco conference for venture capitalists and start-up founders this month to an upbeat electronic song, “Levels” by Avicii, tech stocks were tanking. “Do you have more depressing music, given what’s going on in the market?” he joked.

Mr. Patel, who runs the San Francisco-based market research company SemiAnalysis, said at the conference that investors’ skepticism about the continued pace of revenue growth at OpenAI and Anthropic was one big reason for market turmoil. He predicted those companies would generate more revenue from new business lines, like offering cybersecurity tools and designing chips.

“I myself am a little cuckoo, and I think they actually will hit this, just to be clear,” he said. “But I think many people are a bit skeptical.”

Some A.I. start-up executives said they have noticed a pullback from investors as they consider jumping into their next rounds of funding. Those company leaders are starting to openly acknowledge one awkward reality of the A.I. boom: The technology’s growth has been largely powered by a relatively small number of voracious business customers and consumers who pay for it.

“Eighty percent of the revenue is probably coming from 20 percent of the users. It might even be 90 percent,” said Aravind Srinivas, the chief executive of the Nvidia-backed A.I. start-up Perplexity, at a conference last week hosted by the tech publication, Newcomer.

(The Times has [sued](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/12/05/technology/new-york-times-perplexity-ai-lawsuit.html) Perplexity, accusing it of copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. The company has denied the claims.)

Even as Silicon Valley venture capitalists watched Anthropic’s rocky entry into the public markets, they remained upbeat about the future.

Hemant Taneja, the chief executive of tech investment firm General Catalyst, said he felt relief that Anthropic’s stock price held above the offering price amid “turbulent” markets. Anthropic, he added, was not a one-off example of a venture-funded company that would capitalize on A.I. advances.

“I’m walking away saying: Who’s the next set of founders with the same opportunity?” he said.

Erin Griffith contributed reporting.
